What Access Should You Give a Website Developer?

Follow a fictional Varanasi exporter as it replaces a request for every password with a task-based access map, approval check and revocation register.

By SiteSutra · 06 November 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

What access should you give a website developer? Keep the business as the owner, then invite a named person or service to the exact system with the lowest role that can complete the next approved task. Record who approved it, when it should be reviewed and how it will be removed. Do not place your primary password, recovery codes or two-factor authentication codes in a project brief.

A developer redesigning a page may need a repository or staging account. That does not automatically require domain ownership, billing control, customer records or permanent production administration. Start from the task, check the provider's current roles and expand access only when a documented dependency requires it.

Nisha receives one request for “all the logins”

Imagine Nisha runs a fictional Varanasi handicraft exporter. The business and situation are original planning examples, not a SiteSutra client story or reported result. Her company asks a developer to rebuild the presentation layer of its website while the existing enquiry system remains in place.

The first access request says: “Please send the hosting, domain, website, analytics and email passwords.” Nisha cannot tell which task needs each account, which person will use it or when access will end. The request also mixes site delivery with billing, business email and customer information.

She pauses the request and maps the next milestone instead: inspect the current code, create a redesigned page on staging, submit it for review and prepare an approved release. Each task receives its own system, named recipient, role, acceptance check and review date. The business retains ownership throughout.

Start with systems, not passwords

Nisha makes an inventory of systems the project may touch: domain and DNS, hosting, code repository, content management system, staging environment, production environment, Search Console, analytics, booking or enquiry provider, file storage and any customer-data system. Listing a system does not mean the developer needs access to it.

For every system, she records the business owner, billing owner, recovery method and current administrators. She keeps secrets and recovery information outside the project brief. The inventory answers who controls the asset; the access register answers who needs a temporary working role.

This is distinct from handing over ownership. A business can remain the verified or billing owner while inviting a developer through the provider's user and permission controls. When a platform has no suitable delegated role, Nisha decides whether the business owner can perform the bounded change from reviewed instructions.

Map each task to the smallest practical role

Nisha's hypothetical access map
Approved taskLikely systemAccess decisionBusiness keeps
Review current codeProject repositoryRead access or a reviewed copy when sufficientRepository ownership and settings
Submit implementationProject repositoryNamed contributor with the role required for a branch and pull requestDefault-branch rules and final merge approval
Build and test the redesignStaging environmentProject access without real customer dataProduction access and customer records
Add a DNS verification recordDomain or DNS providerBusiness owner makes one reviewed change, or grants bounded delegation if the provider supports itDomain ownership, billing and recovery
Inspect search performanceSearch ConsoleFull or restricted user according to the exact features requiredVerified ownership and user management
Release an approved buildProduction hostingNamed release role for the approved project and windowAccount ownership, billing and rollback decision

These are planning examples, not universal provider roles. “Editor”, “developer”, “write”, “full user” and “administrator” can mean different things in different systems. Nisha checks the current official permission table before approving an invitation.

Use least privilege as a project rule

OWASP describes least privilege as assigning only the minimum privileges needed to complete a job. It also recommends denying access by default and periodically reviewing permissions so they do not expand unnoticed. For a website project, that means every grant should have an explainable task rather than being added “just in case”.

GitHub, for example, separates repository roles such as Read, Triage, Write, Maintain and Admin, and recommends choosing the role that fits a person's function without giving more access than needed. Admin includes sensitive actions that active coding does not automatically require. The team should inspect the exact provider and repository configuration rather than copy a role name from this article.

Starting smaller also makes escalation clearer. If a build task genuinely needs an additional permission, the developer can identify the blocked action, affected system and duration. Nisha can approve that change as a new decision instead of leaving broad standing access.

Give each person a separate identity

Nisha asks the developer for the account identity used by the provider and sends an invitation from the business-owned account. A shared owner login would make it harder to attribute activity, revoke one person's access or preserve the owner's own recovery route.

She does not email passwords, authentication codes, API keys or recovery codes. When a system needs a secret for an application or deployment pipeline, the project uses the provider's secrets controls and limits who or what can read it. OWASP's secrets-management guidance recommends fine-grained access and warns against leaking secrets through pipeline output.

If a contractor changes, the agency can remove one identity without changing the client's owner account. If the same developer returns for another project, the next scope gets a fresh permission review.

Use staging to reduce production access

The redesign is built with representative, non-sensitive content on staging. Nisha approves responsive layouts, navigation, forms and acceptance checks there. Real customer messages and production databases are not copied into the brief merely to make the page look realistic.

A staging environment does not remove every risk, but it separates routine implementation from live publishing. Production access can be reserved for a named release owner, approved window and rollback plan. When the business can deploy from a reviewed build, the developer may not need standing production administration at all.

For a white-label engagement, the agency remains the client contact and decides which supplier identities can see which project. A developer working on one client should not receive default access to unrelated client repositories, drives or hosting accounts.

Keep verification ownership with the business

Search Console distinguishes owners, full users and restricted users. Google explains that owners have full control, including user management, while full and restricted users have narrower capabilities. A developer who needs to inspect indexing or performance does not automatically need a new ownership token.

Nisha keeps the business as a verified owner and grants the role required for the agreed review. At the end, she removes the user if ongoing access is not part of support. She also reviews unused ownership tokens because Google notes that a former verified owner may regain access while a valid token remains.

The same ownership principle applies across the project: operational access should not silently become business ownership.

Verify access and work separately

Granting an invitation is not proof that the right role works. Nisha asks the recipient to confirm the exact property and permitted action without sharing screenshots that expose private information. The access register records the verification result.

Work acceptance is a separate check. A code change is reviewed in a pull request, a staging page is tested against the brief, a DNS change is confirmed against the approved record and a production release is checked at the public URL. Permission does not approve the work; it only allows an authorised action.

Plan removal before granting access

Every row receives a review trigger: milestone complete, project paused, team member changed, support period ended or scope changed. At handover, Nisha checks users, service accounts, deploy keys, tokens and third-party connections that were created for the project.

Removal should be confirmed in the provider, not assumed from a message. Some credentials are attached to systems rather than a person's membership. GitHub notes, for example, that a deploy key can remain active even after the user who created it leaves an organisation. The handover therefore lists both people and persistent access mechanisms.

If continuing support needs standing access, its purpose, role and review cadence belong in the support agreement. “We may need it later” is not a review schedule.

Review one request before approving it

Use this local planning aid for one system and one task. It does not inspect accounts, grant permissions, save details or determine the exact provider role.

Is this access request ready for approval?

Mark only statements that are documented in the project record.

No checks marked. Begin with the exact system and task.

Keep an access register the owner can inspect

Download the website-developer access register (CSV). Replace the hypothetical rows with the project's real systems, owners, identities, roles, dates, approvals and revocation status.

Do not put passwords, tokens, private keys, customer records or recovery codes in the file. Store it only where the project's authorised people can review it.

Approve the next task, not every possible permission

Nisha grants repository access for the implementation and staging access for review. The business owner handles the bounded DNS change from checked instructions. Production release gets a separate approval, and every project identity receives a handover review.
